title: How China Managed the Oil Shock
gist: Zongyuan Zoe Liu shows how China absorbed the 2026 Strait of Hormuz oil shock by concentrating costs on refiners rather than consumers: capped retail fuel prices and export bans squeezed refining margins, so refiners cut runs and crude imports fell about one-third (to 7.12 mb/d in June) without a government order. Buffers of 1.4 billion barrels of stocks, an EV fleet displacing ~1.35 mb/d and cheaper coal-to-chemicals capacity mean future oil shocks hit China as a managed industrial contraction, and China's restraint softened global oil prices.

themes.theme: China's import cut during the Hormuz shock

insights.claim: Since the February 2026 Strait of Hormuz disruption, which the IEA called the largest supply disruption in oil market history, China did not scramble for replacement barrels and by June had cut crude imports to the lowest level in nearly a decade.
insights.so_what: The world's largest crude importer acted as a demand shock absorber, a key swing factor for oil prices.
insights.quote: the largest supply disruption in the history of the global oil market
insights.locator: Since what the International Energy Agency called
insights.speaker: Zongyuan Zoe Liu

insights.claim: China's crude imports fell about one-third in Q2 2026, from an average 12 million barrels per day (H2 2025 through February) to 8.1 mb/d, bottoming at 7.12 mb/d in June.
insights.so_what: A ~4 mb/d demand drop from one buyer materially offset the global supply loss.
insights.locator: As refiners retreated from the spot crude market
insights.speaker: Zongyuan Zoe Liu

insights.claim: Over Q2 China bought roughly 355 million fewer barrels than at its prewar pace — almost a month of normal imports, or about 180 fully loaded supertankers.
insights.so_what: Quantifies the volume of global demand destruction China contributed; relevant to tanker demand.
insights.locator: During those three months, China bought
insights.speaker: Zongyuan Zoe Liu

insights.claim: China resumed crude imports cautiously in July, but the rebound stayed weak through August and September and far below precrisis levels.
insights.so_what: Chinese demand is not snapping back, capping upside for crude prices as supply recovers.
insights.locator: Since what the International Energy Agency called
insights.speaker: Zongyuan Zoe Liu

insights.claim: The U.S. EIA concluded that China's lower imports reduced global demand and softened upward pressure on oil prices, sparing the world an even more severe squeeze.
insights.so_what: China's policy choices are a first-order driver of global oil price outcomes in supply shocks.
insights.locator: Thus, by concentrating the Hormuz shock downstream
insights.speaker: Zongyuan Zoe Liu

insights.claim: Beijing treats the Hormuz shock as a macro-stability problem, prioritizing avoidance of imported stagflation because its demand-constrained economy cannot withstand cost-push inflation without wage growth.
insights.so_what: Expect Chinese policy to suppress consumer pass-through of energy costs at the expense of corporate margins.
insights.quote: its demand-constrained economy cannot withstand the wrong kind of imported inflation
insights.locator: Chinese leaders view the Hormuz supply shock
insights.speaker: Zongyuan Zoe Liu

insights.claim: A visible rise in living costs would be far harder for Beijing to manage than an industrial adjustment among a concentrated group of refiners, given social-stability pressure from weak jobs and stagnant wages.
insights.so_what: Social stability concerns explain Beijing's choice to concentrate shock costs on industry.
insights.locator: The Chinese political system and its policymakers
insights.speaker: Zongyuan Zoe Liu

insights.claim: In early March China first restricted refined-product exports, then within a week made the sharpest increase in regulated retail fuel price ceilings since 2022; after prices topped $100/bbl in late March it raised ceilings again but avoided full pass-through.
insights.so_what: Chinese product export curbs tighten Asian fuel markets during shocks.
insights.locator: As the crisis hit, Beijing instead
insights.speaker: Zongyuan Zoe Liu

insights.claim: By concentrating the shock downstream at refiners, the government induced a sharp crude import contraction without ever ordering it: refiners facing capped domestic prices and banned exports minimized losses by cutting runs and imports.
insights.so_what: China can engineer demand destruction via price controls, a lever other importers lack.
insights.quote: the Chinese government initially induced a sharp crude imports contraction without commanding it
insights.locator: Thus, by concentrating the Hormuz shock downstream
insights.speaker: Zongyuan Zoe Liu

insights.claim: China entered the disruption with an estimated 1.4 billion barrels of commercial and strategic crude, about 120 days of prewar imports, enough to sustain at least a three-month import cut without a sharp contraction.
insights.so_what: Large stockpiles give Beijing staying power and bargaining leverage in supply crises.
insights.locator: Inventory availability provided the initial buffer
insights.speaker: Zongyuan Zoe Liu

insights.claim: Customs and NBS data suggest Chinese inventory build slowed from January to April and refiners did not need to draw down stocks until May and June.
insights.so_what: Stock drawdowns began late, implying restocking demand could later support crude imports.
insights.locator: At the refiner level, these stocks
insights.speaker: Zongyuan Zoe Liu

insights.claim: China's EV fleet displaced an estimated 1.35 million barrels per day of oil in H1 2026, about 6 percent of total crude imports.
insights.so_what: Electrification structurally reduces China's oil-shock exposure on the fuel side.
insights.locator: Existing electrification helped ensure reduced needs.
insights.speaker: Zongyuan Zoe Liu

insights.claim: Electrification has shifted Chinese crude demand growth from fuels to petrochemical feedstocks, turning an oil shock from a fuel-shortage problem into an industrial-adjustment problem manageable with supply-side tools.
insights.so_what: Petrochemical demand, not transport fuel, is now the marginal driver of Chinese crude imports.
insights.locator: This change has transformed the nature
insights.speaker: Zongyuan Zoe Liu

insights.claim: March 2026 refinery throughput fell to 61.76 million tonnes (about 14.6 mb/d), down 2.2 percent year on year and well below the ~16.3 mb/d available from imports plus domestic output, as refiners preserved inventories.
insights.so_what: Run cuts started early, ahead of physical shortage.
insights.locator: Even though crude secured before the Hormuz
insights.speaker: Zongyuan Zoe Liu

insights.claim: At the worst point in April-May, Shandong teapot refiners lost over 1,200 yuan per tonne processed, a negative margin of roughly $24-25 per barrel.
insights.so_what: Independent refiners bore heavy losses; watch for consolidation and credit stress in the sector.
insights.locator: At the worst point in April and May
insights.speaker: Zongyuan Zoe Liu

insights.claim: Despite NDRC instructions in April not to cut throughput on pain of import-quota cuts, runs contracted sharply; by June Beijing let loss-making teapots cut to no less than 80 percent of 2025 levels, and late-June throughput hit its lowest since COVID.
insights.so_what: Market economics overrode administrative guidance, showing limits of Beijing's control over private refiners.
insights.locator: NBS data shows that refinery throughput contracted
insights.speaker: Zongyuan Zoe Liu

insights.claim: Independent refineries cut output to the lowest since March 2020 and state-owned refiners cut below their own pandemic bottom.
insights.so_what: The adjustment was broad-based across ownership types.
insights.locator: By June, Chinese authorities allowed
insights.speaker: Zongyuan Zoe Liu

insights.claim: In 2025 China produced 15.45 million tonnes of coal-derived olefins (15 percent of national olefin output) and 7.62 million tonnes of coal-derived ethylene glycol (about one-third of national output).
insights.so_what: Coal chemicals provide meaningful substitute capacity, reducing crude-feedstock dependence.
insights.locator: Before the oil supply disruption, China already
insights.speaker: Zongyuan Zoe Liu

insights.claim: In late March-April 2026, coal-based olefins cost about 6,800 yuan per ton versus roughly 10,700 yuan for oil-based production, a cost advantage of more than one-third.
insights.so_what: High crude prices shift Chinese chemical output toward coal, reducing naphtha demand and raising coal demand.
insights.locator: High crude prices weaken the economics
insights.speaker: Zongyuan Zoe Liu

insights.claim: Per NDRC estimates, naphtha makes up about 75 percent of oil-based olefin costs versus coal at about 22 percent of coal-olefin costs, making naphtha crackers far more sensitive to crude prices.
insights.so_what: Structural cost advantage for Chinese coal-to-olefins producers whenever oil is expensive.
insights.locator: The NDRC attributed this gap partly
insights.speaker: Zongyuan Zoe Liu

insights.claim: Chinese policy deliberately built the coal-to-chemicals pathway (2017 NDRC plan) and since 2022 formally promoted 'reducing fuels and increasing chemicals' in the 14th five-year plan.
insights.so_what: Long-run industrial policy explains China's resilience; not an improvised response.
insights.locator: China has deliberately developed this
insights.speaker: Zongyuan Zoe Liu

insights.claim: Chinese refinery-run recovery will depend more on fuel margins, inventory needs and government supply requirements than on crude availability; while petrochemical economics stay poor, integrated refiners have little incentive to return to spot purchases.
insights.so_what: Expect sluggish Chinese spot crude buying even as supply normalizes — bearish for crude prices.
insights.locator: Thus, recovery in refinery runs is likely
insights.speaker: Zongyuan Zoe Liu

insights.claim: Future oil shocks are less likely to trigger an immediate energy crisis in China and more likely to unfold as a managed industrial contraction, with costs compressed among refiners and industrial producers.
insights.so_what: China's oil vulnerability is lower than its import dependence suggests; equity risk sits with refiners/chemicals.
insights.quote: more likely to unfold as a managed industrial contraction
insights.locator: Future oil shocks may be less likely
insights.speaker: Zongyuan Zoe Liu

insights.claim: Import dependence ratios are an incomplete gauge of oil-shock vulnerability; what matters equally is how deeply and how long a country can cut imports before industrial damage or intolerable costs.
insights.so_what: Reassess country energy-risk models using import-cut capacity rather than dependence ratios alone.
insights.quote: An import dependence ratio alone is therefore an incomplete measure
